title: berit
summary: These references present covenant in different settings. Genesis 9 describes God’s covenant with Noah and every living creature after the flood. Deuteronomy 6 places Israel’s daily teaching and obedience within its covenant life. Jeremiah 31 promises a renewed covenant with Israel and Judah, and Hebrews 8 quotes that promise in its argument about Jesus’ ministry. The passages show why covenant cannot be reduced to one formula: it can name a promise, a relationship, or the framework for a community’s life.
historical_context: The passages range from the post-flood narrative in Genesis to Moses’ instruction in Deuteronomy, prophetic restoration language in Jeremiah, and Hebrews’ use of Jeremiah. These are the textual settings represented in the source list; no specific treaty comparison is needed to explain them.
canonical_context: Genesis 9 locates covenant in God’s promise concerning the earth after the flood. Deuteronomy 6 shows Israel’s instruction and loyalty within its covenant story. Jeremiah 31 promises a renewed relationship marked by internalized instruction and forgiveness; Hebrews 8 quotes that passage and interprets it in relation to Jesus. The sequence connects narrative, instruction, prophetic hope, and later interpretation without making their uses identical.
literary_context: Genesis narrates a covenant promise, Deuteronomy gives covenant instruction, Jeremiah speaks a prophetic promise, and Hebrews quotes that promise in an extended argument. The forms help explain the differences: one passage establishes a promise, another teaches a way of life, and later passages announce and interpret renewal.
covenantal_significance: The references trace covenant language from a promise to Noah, through Israel’s instruction, to Jeremiah’s promise of renewal and Hebrews’ interpretation of it. The reader can see both continuity and change in what each text emphasizes: preservation, faithful life, forgiveness, and renewed knowledge of God.
canonical_role: This entry gathers passages that use covenant language in narrative, instruction, prophetic promise, and New Testament interpretation. Its references show a developing theme while preserving the distinct claims made in each text.
